newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Holidaymakers flee as storms lash New Zealand.
newsitem.headline: Holidaymakers flee as storms lash New Zealand.

text.p: Thousands of holidaymakers fled their campsites and civil defence officials declared emergencies in some regions as the remnants of tropical Cyclone Fergus lashed New Zealand on Monday.
Floods closed major arterial routes and high winds felled trees and brought down power and telephone lines in some areas.

Jim Hilbron, operations officer at the Ministry of Civil Defence, said the North Island districts of Thames-Coromandel, Hauraki and Matamata-Piako had declared a state of emergency in the country's worst storm since Cyclone Bola in 1988.

"What prompted it mainly was police concern about the welfare of holidaymakers stranded in those areas," Hilbron said. But apart from landslips and flooding on roads, the ministry was not aware of any casualties or major damage.
Meteorologists downgraded Fergus from a cyclone to a "very deep depression" as it bore down on New Zealand, but it still brought torrential rain and wind gusts up to 130 kph (80 mph).

Civil defence authorities urged people in the worst-affected areas to stay indoors and listen to radio bulletins for weather information. Diehard campers were urged to pitch their tents away from rivers, streams and estuaries.

Thousands of people fled the popular resorts of the Bay of Islands and Coromandel Peninsula at the height of the summer holiday season, but many had their escape routes blocked as floods closed major highways.
The Coromandel, east of Auckland, was virtually cut off as rain fell at the rate of 34 mm (1.3 inches) an hour.
In the town of Kerikeri, 1,500 Youth for Christ campers went home, and in the Hunua Ranges, southeast of Auckland, 140 children and 60 adults were evacuated from another camp.
The full force of the storm had yet to hit the northeastern Bay of Plenty region, where television news showed residents placing sandbags to defend against high tide.
Ports and marinas were packed as trawlers, commercial boats and yachts took refuge, but the leading yacht in a round-the-world race arrived safely in Wellington.

Race leader Group 4 sailed into Wellington harbour a day after four people were killed and a fifth went missing in a collision between a container ship and fishing boat. The accident occurred in calm, clear conditions on Sunday evening.

Organisers of the BT Global Challenge race said the other 13 yachts, which have been sailing for 40 days from Rio de Janeiro, were braced for rough seas but were used to severe conditions in the course of their round-the-world voyage.
